newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - German, UK rate fever to dominate.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - German, UK rate fever to dominate.

text.p: Interest rate speculation in Germany and Britain will be the driving force behind financial markets this week, economists said on Friday.
A dearth of data in the U.S. leaves the quarterly refunding auctions as the main focus there in a market that was looking increasingly vulnerable after Friday's strong U.S. payrolls data, they said.

"In Europe, we've got reasonably chunky German data -- industrial production and unemployment. But that will be no more than a side issue to what Buba will do to the repo," said Eric Fishwick, international economist at Nikko Europe in London.
Speculation the Bundesbank may have to act to support the faltering mark will come to a head on Tuesday when the central bank is due to set its repo rate for the next two weeks.

In announcing fixed 3.0 percent repos for just a fortnight last Thursday, ahead of a four-week summer break, the Bundesbank sparked talk it was leaving its options open for the second half of the holiday.
But economists said a rise in record low rates was highly unlikely.
"It would be the first German tightening for such a long time, they're unlikely to chose to do it without a council meeting," said Fishwick.
Neil Mackinnon, chief economist at Citibank in London, agreed the possible change in Buba's money market operations would be a key influence in the week.

"If they do...have an aggressive change of tack on interest rates, it could have a knock on effect in Europe and the U.S., particularly for those ERM currencies which may be compelled to follow suit -- that might create some strains there."
Britain's monetary policy committee meeting on Wednesday and Thursday will also keep markets on tenterhooks as bonds dither over the chances of another interest rate rise.
"Things aren't as clear cut as in previous meetings for the direction on rates," said Mackinnon. "My guess is there'll be no change."
Economists said with sterling stubbornly holding above the three mark rate, the Bank of England may be reluctant to encourage further appreciation and intensify pressure on exporters.
They said British June industrial production and manufacturing output data due on Tuesday may show more moderate growth under the burden of a strong pound.
In Germany, key June industrial production data is due out sometime between Monday and Wednesday and July unemployment data will be released on Wednesday.

The spotlight in the U.S. will fall on the refunding auctions with June leading indicators on Tuesday, the Fed's Beige Book of economic conditions on Wednesday and June consumer credit data on Thursday almost the only data to be released.
The Treasury is due to auction $16.0 billion in three-year notes on Tuesday, $12.0 billion of 10-year notes on Wednesday and $10.0 billion of 30-year bonds the following week.
Graham McDevitt, head of bond strategy at Paribas Capital Markets in London, said the Treasury market may be vulnerable to a correction.

"With the refunding next week, the view is in the short term, unless we close above 116-28 (in the September future)...it is very likely that next week we'll have a correction in the market as the auction is taken on board," he said on Friday.
"We had strong employment figures (on Friday), reasonably strong personal income, and with the supply taken on board at these low levels, the balance of risk at the moment is on the downside."

In Japan, the yen current account balance for June is due next week, which analysts said could reignite old tensions with the US. Japanese household spending is due on Tuesday, wholesale prices on Thursday and machinery orders on Friday.
